utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, we will be through very quickly. I would like to ask you for a few more points of clarification. You mentioned yesterday, when we were asking about any statements that you had made after going to Travnik, that you spoke to some people regarding certain studies or books and the like. Did you perhaps discuss the topic at all with Mr. Enes Surkovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First of all, let me correct you. I went from Vitez to Zenica, and not to Travnik, as you said. And I did discuss the topic, because Mr. Enes was collecting information, and he asked me for some photographs, because he was the person in charge of studying the crimes committed against the Bosniaks in the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for mis-speaking and saying "Travnik" instead of Zenica. I know you went to Zenica. So Mr. Surkovic asked you for an interview in his official capacities?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who gave him that assignment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Personally, I know that he collected data from all people who experienced a tragedy like mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also drew attention to an error in the death certificate for your late husband where the date of his death was incorrectly stated. I wanted to ask you, did you, yourself, establish the error and ask for it to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you perhaps discover that this was not the only such case, that there were others?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I knew about this error. I wanted it to be corrected. I have a new death certificate stating the date of death as the 17th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You hadn't heard that the office issuing such certificates had a series of such errors?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I really wasn't interested in that, nor did I hear of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well; thank you. Regarding the HVO soldiers who came to your house, when you came back to collect some things, tell me, could you recognise anyone by name or his face as a local man?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I certainly could not recognise any one of them, but I assumed that the man who watched over us and who said that we should be left alone because we were women and children, he must have known me, because that young man pointed to me, saying, "There's that older woman." I personally didn't know him, maybe by sight, but I am unable to say that I really knew who the man was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you assume that only one of them may have been a local man, but you cannot claim that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot, but on the basis of what he said, I assumed that he must have known me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to remind you, without showing you the statement, in order to save time: In your statement to the investigators given on the 3rd and 4th of March, 1999, you said that you took shelter in Mr. Vlado's house, and only here yesterday in your testimony, or rather talking to the Prosecutor before coming into the courtroom, you explained that the surname of that man was Ramljak?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, at the time you were making that first statement, when you just mentioned him by first name, Vlado, without his surname, is it because you couldn't remember the surname at the time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the time I was making the statement, I just thought it was sufficient to give the name Vlado, because I really did know that his name was Vlado. But before coming here, I asked my brother, because he was also his friend, I asked my brother what his last name was, and he told me it was Ramljak. And that is how I established that the man's surname was Ramljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So will you confirm, is my conclusion right, when you made your first statement in March 1999, you were sure that his name was Vlado; later on, you checked and learnt that his surname is Ramljak?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The course of events on the 16th, and then you reached Divjak on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me where exactly in Divjak? Which locality, which house, what part of the settlement?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In front of Franjo Pocrnja's house, across the road from the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the one side is the Pocrnja house and restaurant, and the other side of the street is the entrance to the UNPROFOR base; who brought you there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Bruno Buzuk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you reached that spot, there were no HVO soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that moment, the situation was quite normal. There were some HVO soldiers, but they didn't provoke us in any way at that time, when we got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, could you tell us when this idea of an exchange was mentioned for the first time and by whom?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First, unofficially, Franjo Pocrnja said that his son, Zoran Pocrnja, was in Zenica. He happened to be in the hospital with his wife for some examinations. And that was a talk between me and him, and he said, "It would be fine if I could exchange my son for you." But this wasn't stated in the presence of UNPROFOR or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were no HVO soldiers there present at that time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not at that point in time. There were some soldiers, but they didn't cause any trouble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the son of Pocrnja, Zoran; are you referring to the gynaecologist, a physician?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Zenica with his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he, as a Croat, would not be released from Zenica; was that the point?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why then the exchange?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think -- I don't think, I'm sure, that it was a misunderstanding on the part of his father that his son could be captured because he happened to be in Zenica. But he lived -- normally he was not under arrest, but it was his understanding that we could leave and that his son could come back, because the roads were already blocked. There were conflicts, and it was -- one couldn't travel normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. The road was blocked, but did anyone tell you that you were not allowed to leave Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because of the tragedy I had experienced, I wanted to stay in Vitez municipality. I never thought about my own destiny and what would happen to me in Vitez, but when Bruno came to fetch the wife of Dr. Patkovic and to transfer her to the Pocrnja house, or rather the UNPROFOR compound, I asked that he take us as well -- that is, me and my children -- and he did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, nobody offered you to leave, but you asked to leave?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is when you had that conversation with Pocrnja?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, Bruno simply drove us there so that UNPROFOR could transfer us to Travnik when the occasion arose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This place directly opposite to the entrance of the UN base, it is visible for the UN guards standing there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is visible. They have a good view. Yes, it is a very short distance separating them; just the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When those HVO soldiers approached you, then you said assaulted you, threatened you, et cetera, did the UNPROFOR soldiers intervene who saw all this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did intervene. A man sat with us. Whether he was a major or not, I don't know. He was sitting with my children and holding them by the hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask your permission. We just presume, because we didn't have any data in advance, that it might be this position, and we drew a simple sketch. But unfortunately we weren't able to copy it. Just for ease of reference, could we place it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, put it on the ELMO. It's not coming up on mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Neither on ours. Okay, we can leave it. So later if we have the picture -- yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Mahmutovic, will you please look at this sketch? That's good, that's good. A little bit up so we can see the house on the other side of the street. Yes, that will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, would it be possible to know who made this sketch, who drew it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Defence, we. Me, myself. It's just a simple drawing to show there at the time, nothing else. It's not the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam Mahmutovic, will you show us the entrance to the UN base, please? Just point to it with the pointer, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For me, this whole area could be the entrance (indicating). This fence, roughly there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point to the right on the drawing below the ELMO? Show us the entrance. Is that the entrance?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. The UNPROFOR base was there (indicating), yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is where the guards were?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Believe me, I really didn't enquire nor look around. I wasn't in such a state of mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is a schematic presentation of the house across the road. It bears the number "6". Does it correspond to the position of the Pocrnja house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Roughly, it is somewhere there. I'm not sure that it should be parallel with the road or, rather, at right angles to the road. I'm not sure of that, but roughly like that. It was somewhere there (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) So the way the diagram shows it, the house is opposite the entrance to the UN base. Thank you. (In English) Your Honour, if the Court orders so, we can put that in evidence. Of course, we will copy it immediately after the day. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. If you want to produce a sketch plan, you can do it in your own evidence in chief. Meanwhile, the witness hasn't recognised enough of it to make it her own document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Your Honour, yes. The idea was really to save the time, to have the picture instead of too much talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were sitting somewhere there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in the yard of the Pocrnja house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This UN officer joined you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that officer was there, these threats and insults were hurled at you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Cerkez appeared?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see where he had come from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You had the drawing. He came along the road towards us. He came towards us. He passed by the entrance to the UNPROFOR base. He was coming from the main Vitez-to-Travnik road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As if he had come out of the base or from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, really I don't know where he had come from. I just saw him appear in front of us, and the soldiers started saying, "Here is Cerkez." In fact, I saw him myself. There was several other soldiers with him when he appeared. Where he had come from, I don't know. Whether he had come from the UNPROFOR base or from his own car, I really don't know, but I saw him in person approaching us or, rather, the group of soldiers who were in our immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Was he approaching alone or with someone?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was approaching with two or three soldiers. I think Franjo Pocrnja's son-in-law was there too. I know that that man was killed. I also know that he too was a good friend of my husband's, but I can't remember his name. I really knew him and I recognised him, and I expected him to lend us a hand, as I did Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those people with Cerkez in uniform?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they bear Viteska Brigade insignia; did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you conclude in any way that Cerkez was the commander of those who were with him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were HVO members. I knew that Cerkez was an HVO commander, because I lived and worked there and I simply recognised him. Probably he was the commander of those men too, because he first addressed them and then us. He first approached those soldiers who were standing next to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that those soldiers were furious and angry. Did any one of them mention that any one of theirs had got killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those soldiers were insulting us. They wanted to strangle one of my children, then the other. He said that somebody had got killed. Anyway, one or two bodies of Croats needed to be exchanged, and apparently the army would not allow it, and they were furious. They were offering the five of us, myself, my two daughters, Mrs. Besa and her son, and the dead body of my husband, to be exchanged in front of the UNPROFOR, but the army apparently did not allow it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they had already learned about your agreement with Pocrnja and Buzuk?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. The discussion with Pocrnja was just a friendly conversation. I don't know whether Pocrnja said anything to those soldiers, but I don't believe so. That conversation has nothing to do with what happened here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those soldiers, were they people living in Divjak?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were mostly young men whom I cannot really identify. I cannot say that they were so and so, their names. But they were people there. Their wives were there, their houses were there. As for those that I have identified, that is, Dragan and Braco, Budimir, them I know in person, and they insulted me the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, this Braco, was that the ambulance driver?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. No, unless he may have been during the time of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he's not the same one, so you don't know his surname?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Budimir. He's the brother of Dragan Budimir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This place in front of Pocrnja's house is the place where locals would gather, men and women?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were several houses nearby, and there were two of my friends, Croats, who worked with me. They were standing there too and watching what was going on, and they were actually talking to those soldiers who were there, who were threatening us. One soldier stood in front of us, pointed a rifle at us. He was wearing an HVO uniform, and he said that we would be killed. He said to Besa, "You were with them, you ate with them, and you will be killed with them." He was sitting in front of us with a gun pointed at us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in time, did this UNPROFOR officer react in any way to prevent this or to calm things down?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My older daughter, she could speak English, she was in 8th grade, and I told her to tell the gentleman from UNPROFOR what was going on, that her father had been killed, that her house had been burned down. He consoled her and told her not to be afraid, that they would all disappear upon his order. But they kept saying, "We're not afraid of UNPROFOR. You think you're safe because you're in front of the UNPROFOR base, but that is no security at all for you." That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you went on to say that you were transferred by small bus from there, and who transferred you; UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, a local man. A Muslim who stayed behind, who hadn't left yet, he was a bus driver. He had his own bus, and in agreement with those soldiers, he often went to the line of separation. He talked to the army for an exchange to take place, and no agreement could be made until the main person in charge of UNPROFOR, who was in Busovaca, he probably intervened and organised the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you were transferred to the part of Divjak known as Sadovaca?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was transferred to the separation line, the farm at Divjak where the actual exchange was carried out, and then with this bus I went on to the place called Sadovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is where you entered the territory under BH army control. From then on, you were in the territory controlled by the BH army. My question is why did you have to go on foot?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: How else, when I had to cross the hills? There were no cars, no roads. How could I reach those places? This place is in the mountains, and there was no other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The BH army didn't give you any assistance?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My brother-in-law lived nearby. I spent the night there. It may have been 12.00 or 1.00. Anyway, it was rather late, and I was taken in by soldiers who were nearby, army soldiers, the BH army soldiers, and they took me to my brother-in-law's house, who in the morning escorted us on foot, myself and my daughters, to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One further question. Regarding all those talks over the exchange, which obviously went on all day, the accused Mario Cerkez, did he in any sense participate in those talks about the exchange, directly or indirectly, or did you hear that he participated?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not hear whether he did participate or not. I don't know, but I know the words that he told us, which I have told you and which you don't want me to repeat. As the HVO commander, who else could have participated but he in the exchange? If the most important person from the UNPROFOR in Busovaca had to come to resolve the situation, who else could have spoken on behalf of the HVO but he?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that Mario Cerkez negotiated the exchange?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone negotiating, nor do I know where they negotiated. All I know is that this major who was watching us said, "Negotiations will be conducted; don't worry." All I saw was when Mario appeared and what he said. Whether he negotiated or not, I don't know, but we were exchanged in the evening.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn later on that there was an HVO command based in the hotel in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NUSRETA MAHMUTOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was their main stronghold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it disputed, Mr. Kovacic, that Mr. Cerkez said that as far as he was concerned, to the soldiers, you could kill them all, but UNPROFOR and the BBC were here, and the Armija would gain an advantage? Is it challenged that that was said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No. The statement is correct, but the statement, you of course notice, has indeed two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll go into that. That sounds to be the subject of argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is another issue. What is disputed is only the context of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) We will show in our Defence what exactly the context was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, the Office of the Prosecutor has no further questions. The Office of the Prosecutor, with your permission, would just like to have a clarification regarding a possibility that could be granted by the Chamber. Following Mrs. Mahmutovic's testimony, and because of the questions raised regarding this press conference in Busovaca on the 15th of April, 1993, the Office of the Prosecutor would ask if it is possible, because we consider that this would be the best opportunity to do so, to present the press conference or at least an abstract from it, chosen by the Office of the Prosecutor, with the appropriate transcript, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think you probably should do it through an appropriate witness. When you come across a witness who saw it, or something of that sort, you can call it through them, rather than this witness, who merely heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That is quite correct, Mr. President. The Office of the Prosecutor was just wondering whether it was necessary for the witness to be present for the video to be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this witness certainly needn't be present, because she didn't see it. Mrs. Mahmutovic, thank you very much for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded, so you are released, if you would like to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, you might like to consider an appropriate moment to introduce this video; I'm by no means certain that this is. If you've got another witness, we'll hear the witness, and then in due course you can produce the video of the press conference; ideally, through somebody who actually saw it, if you've got such a witness. Otherwise, we'll consider having it admitted as a documentary exhibit. But it may be you could discuss it with the Defence and find a suitable time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I fully understand your position, Mr. President. We are not certain of having a witness, at least not one that is available, who could assist with the showing of this press conference. On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, I request permission from your Chamber, and I do so because the question was raised yesterday during the testimony, and especially as during the testimony of another witness on the 14th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have not made myself plain. At the moment, no. When you find an appropriate witness to do it, we will admit it. If you can't find an appropriate witness, we'll consider admitting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, can we go on with the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Lopez-Terres, before the next witness, for whom you have given us a summary, as usual, on the basis of the statement which will help you to guide the examination-in-chief, and which I have in front of me, I am sorry that I didn't have it yesterday. This may be a more general observation. The Chamber would like to have this type of document in advance and not five minutes before the witness enters the courtroom. A second point is that there are certain aspects here regarding which we have already had testimony: for example, the Kaonik, the Vitez cinema. I think that the Office of the Prosecutor should lead this evidence so as to avoid repetition of a certain number of facts which have already been provided by others before this Chamber. Corroboration of certain points is not absolutely necessary, such as those regarding Kaonik or the Vitez cinema. Therefore, in this testimony -- and this also applies to the cross-examination -- we go directly to the main points of the charges, rather than giving us a general overview which distances us, sometimes, from the main points. That would be my suggestion, and I think that is something that everyone should bear in mind in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I fully accept your comments and your criticism in my personal name and on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I should like to specify, however, that my colleague, Madam Somers, will be examining the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no criticism, but perhaps we could move as rapidly as possible, particularly on the points where there has been no dispute, such as about what happened in Kaonik and, as far as I remember, the cinema. I might point out, in addition to what the Judge has said, we have already heard at least four witnesses about Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court -- I'm sorry to interrupt -- relative to next witness, I make an application as follows. There are two official statements from this witness. There is a third, however, which is critical to the Defence, which I rise to inform you about. The first statement is a statement dated August 31, 1995, on the international criminal tribunal for the prosecution of persons criminally -- persons responsible for serious violations, et cetera, and it's roughly 7 pages. The next is a February 13, 1997, statement of roughly three or four pages, properly served in English and in B/C/S. There is however, Judge, an October 4, 1994, statement given in Zenica, in front of the tribunal about which you've already heard that was investigating crimes. It is in Croatian. It is roughly nine pages, single-spaced. It was provided to us on 31 May, 1999, just in Croatian. We have yet to receive an English translation. It is our position that the Office of the Prosecutor is not in compliance with the Court's order relative to this very important document. It's important, I might add, because it is so full and rich of information. It is important because it was given closest in time and closest in proximity to the events, a comment alluded to in private correspondence between Mr. Nice and myself in which he notes that witness statements closer in time and closer in proximity are to be heavily relied on, something I don't think there is much argument about. It was in a court. It was under oath. There was a judge. And it's important. We are unable to use it fully, although -- I will be perfectly candid with the Court; I have looked through the document for the name "Dario Kordic," I can figure that out, and any time I saw that, I asked what the words around that particular paragraph were. But we don't have it in full, and so I ask that Your Honour consider either precluding the Prosecution from putting on this witness, or alternatively, if the witness is allowed to testify -- and I will be cross-examining, and I am prepared to proceed -- but if it turns out, when we do get the translation, which I gather was given to the Translation Unit, that there are areas for exploration, then that the witness be called back. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear the witness now, and if there is an application to recall the witness arising out of matters in the statement, which is only in Croatian, as we understand it, then we will consider that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And I trust the Office of the Prosecutor is continuing to get the translation for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That is correct. (Witness entered courtroom)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat. Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please state your full and complete name.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Enes Surkovic. I'm a mechanical engineer, born on March 2nd, 1994, in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your background, sir?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Bosniak, of the Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever served in the military in your country?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I served in the navy in 1972, from '72 to '73.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of work have you done since you finished your university?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a graduate of the third gymnasium in Sarajevo. My parents lived in Konjic. We have our own land. During the holidays I would help my parents in the field work. When I was in high school, I liked to travel a lot as a student also, so I did travel a little bit more around the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could be a little more precise, once you graduated from the engineering faculty, what professional positions did you hold?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't suppose there is any dispute about that, if you would like to summarise it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you worked as a teacher in high school as well as in the business section?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I misunderstood. I thought that you were asking what I did when I was in high school. After I graduated, I worked in Vitez for about 20 years, 15 of which I worked as a professor in the Vitez high school, and the rest I worked as a mechanical engineer, as an official in a factory, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a teacher in Vitez high school, did you ever come across Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was my pupil. I knew Mr. Kordic very well when he was a pupil, from his days as a pupil, and I can say that Kordic belonged to a very bright generation of pupils in the Vitez high school. I know that Mr. Kordic would come by bus from Busovaca to Vitez to school. He was a good student in his grades and also in his behaviour. I remember certain pupils from his class, from his generation, and I know that some of those young men are already scientific workers, and they are teaching at university in Sarajevo. I know Mr. Kordic graduated from university, but from about 1978, '79, when he completed high school, I never saw or met Mr. Kordic again. But only in 1990 and after that, I more and more frequently used to hear certain information about Mr. Kordic. I think he became a little more politically active. Since then, I had a little more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt you, Mr. Surkovic. This is all information you received. Let's go to 1993, shall we, paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, I don't think these matters have been in dispute, so you can take them fairly briefly, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, will the Court permit me to take one digression back so we can establish one aspect of his position in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, besides being a resident of the municipality of Vitez, were you politically active, and if so, could you explain a little bit about the nature of your political activity?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was. At that time during Tito's Yugoslavia, the Communist Party was the leading political force in Yugoslavia, and at that time -- this is around 1980 -- I was the president of the municipal committee of the League of Communists in Vitez. After that, I was a member of the socio-political council and the intermunicipal conference of the municipalities of Vitez, Travnik, and Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the group that was principally formed from the League of Communists acquire a new party name after the elections, and if so, would you please tell us what it was? Is the SDP party a carry-over from that original group?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Many are mistaken about this. SDP is no development from the League of Communists, it's a completely new political party, a new political party that I still belong to today and that I belonged to in 1990, after the first multi-party elections in Vitez. The political party comprises Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, and other nations and nationalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, based on your being a political person in your municipality, did you have any difficulties mingling with members of other ethnic groups prior to 1993? Was there generally good co-operation between and among the ethnic groups within your municipality?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't say anything good about this. I would like to emphasise that at the first multi-party elections in Vitez, the national parties, the HDZ and the SDA, had a convincing victory. So already in 1991, these leading political parties, the HDZ and the SDA, started to disagree. There were certain disagreements about the organisation of the political life in the municipality, also the distribution of the political offices. These conflicts deepened, according to people who were politically active in those parties at the time, leading officials. Professor Munib Kajmovic worked with me. He was the professor at the high school. He was the president of the SDA party. Also Mr. Anto Valenta, who was one of the leading HDZ party officials. There were claims that the HDZ was seeking to get more political power than it was entitled according to the results of the elections, and in reflection to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, we've heard a great deal of evidence about this. This is no criticism of you, of course. But, Ms. Somers, let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, could you indicate what happened to you and your family on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that you have heard similar testimony, but on the 16th of April, at 5.30, we were woken up by detonations and firing from automatic weapons. We knew that something was wrong. Everybody, every reasonable man, would know that tensions in Vitez had grown. I went to get my children. We went to the shelter in our basement. The door was unlocked. The light was on. There were several more people there; Croats, Muslims, also some Serbs. We were all in the basement. Around 6.00, somebody knocked on the front door. They pounded on the front door. People were afraid. Nobody wanted to go to open the front door. I went, but my neighbour, the wife of Franjo Franjic, held me back. She said, "Professor, don't go to open the door. I'll do it." So she went to open the door. I stayed in the basement. She came back, followed by three men. They wanted the owners of the houses to unlock their houses, to unlock their apartments. When I opened my apartment, when I opened the door, the door was already opened. I saw a young man there. He had a black mask on his face. My oldest son was standing next to him. My son was probably nervous. He was a second-year student in the high school. I had lost control over him. I saw an automatic rifle in the hands of that soldier, and I was afraid for my boy. I asked him to go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, excuse me. Could I ask you, were you able to identify what type of soldier it was, from what military?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: The men had HVO insignia. They were HVO soldiers. The young man who had a sock on his head, I think that was a young man from Vitez. He could have even been my pupil, my student. I think the masked boys were those who were from Vitez, but there were also men with no masks or socks on their heads or camouflage paint, and they were probably not from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, did any of the soldiers who came to your apartment take anything from your apartment? Was there something that they were particularly interested in that you could give them?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The man who was in my apartment at that time was searching through the cupboard in my kitchen. He was looking for something. I knew what he was looking for. I knew he was looking for my pistol. I had a license for a gun. But I had moved the gun from the cupboard, because I knew that they would be looking for weapons. Based on my earlier experience, I knew. The young man clearly couldn't find the gun. He spent -- he found a watch there. There was some money there, maybe one or two hundred German marks. It wasn't important. But I told them, "If you're looking for weapons, they are not there. I moved the weapon. It's in the washing machine in the bathroom." I just wanted to use that opportunity. That young man was nervous, and I thought -- I could see that, because he pointed the automatic rifle at me. I told my boy to go to the basement. The soldier went to the bathroom. My neighbour was standing next to me, and he asked me to go to the cellar. He assumed that something really --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, did they in fact take anything from your apartment that you know about for sure? Did you give up a weapon? Did you lose any valuables?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The man found my gun in the washing machine. He took that. I told -- I already said that he took an old watch that was a memento. He also took some money. I didn't have a lot of money, there was a crisis already, so the amount of money was negligible. But he found it and he took it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, you mentioned a few minutes ago that based on your prior experience, you knew what they were looking for. Could you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: The first conflict between the army and the HVO took place on October 20th, 1992, in Vitez. After that conflict, HVO patrols would enter apartments of certain Muslim families. I know a man. His name is Zaim Zukan, nicknamed Pozicija. They came to his door. He wasn't at home. But he was a hunter. His son was home. The men who came put a bomb into his mouth, asking him to tell them where his father's weapons were. Then the host came. He saved his child. He gave them the hunting rifle. That is how I know that they would be looking for weapons, and there were other such examples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, were you in a group that has been referred to as a group of prominent citizens who were incarcerated in various locations in Vitez and in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: That day, at about 10.00, residents from my building -- there are about 20 apartments there -- we went to the basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mrs. Somers, could you please -- can you hear me? Could you ask the witness to answer the questions you're asking him, because he has not answered your question. We would like the witness to answer questions put to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps it wasn't clear. Let me repeat a few, Mr. Surkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you among --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in that group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for cutting you off. Would you be kind enough, if you can, to enumerate some of the names of the people who were also in that group? If you know all of them, that would be fine, but as many as you can recollect.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: There was Dr. Patkovic, Dr. Mahmutovic, Professor Muragamula Halilovic (phoen), Professor Hodzic, Professor Muhamed Kaleta (phoen), Professor Zisko Hajrudin, Engineer Dzevad Ridzanovic. He is a master of sciences. There was a lot of people, university people, regular workers, who were all captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also in the company of Mr. Fuad Kakjno, Mr. Bahtija Sivro, and Mr. Serif Causevic, Mr. Alija Basic?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those people were with me, but this is a group of 13 people which, on May 5th, were taken from Vitez to Kaonik. Mr. Fuad Kakjno, Bahtija Sivro, Serif Causevic, Alija Basic, Suad Salkic, and others were there. There were 13 of us altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just returning quickly to the 16th of April, were you aware of something terrible happening to Mr. Omerdic, and if so, could you briefly tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: When I went to the cellar, the basement, with my boy, I could hear shooting on the floors of the building that I lived in. I asked a friend of mine, Mr. Ilija Azinovic, to go with me to see what was happening, because I knew that somebody had been shot. We went to the late Salih Omerdic's apartment. A man was lying there in a puddle of blood. He was shot by a bullet here, indicates --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Inaudible]... to Mr. Omerdic, the man you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Salih Omerdic, he had a stab wound in his neck, this part, the part of the neck. The neck was not slit, but the knife had gone clean through. I had thought that maybe we could help him, but when I saw a big puddle of blood underneath his head and I could see that he was giving no signs of life, I knew that we couldn't help him. So with my friend, Ilija Azinovic, we laid him down on the ground. We closed his eyes and his mouth. We covered him with a sheet. Then he had the difficult part of going to tell his parent what happened. Mr. Ilija Azinovic is a Croat, but he cried, because his children went to the same class as the children of the man who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mrs. Omerdic in the apartment, and if so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, no, I think we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next page, really. The witness has said that he was incarcerated. It seems he was taken, is this right, to the university, put in the basement there?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence about that and the conditions that were there. Then he was in the cinema. Is that right, Mr. Surkovic? That's where you went?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same building, but it's the basement rooms. They are in another part of the building, and the cinema hall is to the right. But it's the same building, under the same roof, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were short, as far as rations were concerned, and there were a lot of you kept in the same room?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of people. We had one tin of sardines and a quarter of bread, that was all, but our families were permitted to bring us food. Yes, there were a lot of people. It wasn't just one room, it was the cinema hall, the basement facilities, and it was the former offices of the League of Communists were on the top floor. So detained in those facilities were about 300 to 320 of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then we've heard evidence that you were among the group taken to the chess club, and then --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- you stayed there two days.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then you were transferred to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers. If there's anything that you would like to ask about Kaonik which will add something, you, of course, do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, I will. If I may just ask about four names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Surkovic, if you recognise the names Zdravko Jurcevic, Zlatko Nakic, and Dragan Toljusic? If you do recognise those names, who were they?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Zdravko Jurcevic and Dragan Toljusic are former students of mine. They are boys who worked as security guards at the Workers' University. On the top floor -- on the first floor of that Workers' University are the offices of the HVO, but also there were some detainees there. Zlatko Nakic, I think he was the chief of police. Unfortunately, that young man was killed in the war. He was the chief. Sometimes I would see him around the Workers' University.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in any way connected to your stay in the cinema or any connection to your incarceration?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: These men -- I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these individuals guarding you or associated in any way with your incarceration or detention in the cinema in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that Zdravko Jurcevic was a very fair person. He was my pupil. I can't say the same for Dragan Toljusic. The men are very different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll just ask you directly. Were they --

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is [inaudible]?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: That was one of the men from the police. I would see him often. He knew me. He was a pretty strict man, but I can say that in my presence, he never beat any of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "police", can you identify which police department or units you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: HVO police. They were securing those premises. If you will permit me, regarding our return from Busovaca, I have some additional information regarding the work of the police. The work of the police who were there before I went to Busovaca, I have no objections to the way they worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you got to Busovaca, which would be the reference to Kaonik, were you personally ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They didn't interrogate me, but they did ask Fuad Kakjno, Serif Causevic, and Bahtija Sivro and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware or have you been made aware of the presence of Darko Kraljevic in Kaonik present at any of the interrogations of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I know a couple of the men who were doing the security work in the Kaonik prison. I do not wish to name those men. They are very dear to me. They are Croatian nationality, and they were very upset by the capture of my colleagues and myself. They would bring me food and coffee and they took risks, and I didn't expect that. But I know that Darko Kraljevic -- I hope you know that he was killed. But I know that one of those men, when the name of Darko Kraljevic was mentioned, and this man was a pupil of mine, he said, "Hopefully, Darko will not come among us here." I don't know why, if Darko had done something in Busovaca or not, but I could see that those men of Croatian nationality, the guards, were afraid of Darko Kraljevic. I didn't know Darko very well personally, but I could tell that they would not be happy if he were to come to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back to my original question, do you know whether or not or did Alija Basic mention the presence of Darko Kraljevic at all in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Basic was the director of Sintevit in Vitez. It's an enterprise of about 500 or 600 workers. The late Darko Kraljevic was conducting an investigation about the export of explosives and gunpowder. There were two big factories in Vitez of explosives and gunpowder. Darko Kraljevic had found out that some Croat official from Vitez was involved in the smuggling of gunpowder and explosives from Vitez to Croatia, and he thought that Alija Basic could help him to find out something more about this. Alija Basic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard enough about that, unless there's some particular point, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: He has reached the point for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that the Red Cross, Mr. Surkovic, came to visit the prison, and we've heard about their visit. If you get to paragraph 25, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, on or about the 15th of May, you were to have been exchanged. Were you, in fact, exchanged that day, and if so, could you tell us what occurred prior to your leaving the camp?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: We were to have been exchanged then, and we were told to get ready. We saw a Kombi van waiting in front of the door of the building with the 20 cells in it, and Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski called us out one by one to sign some papers on our discharge and sending us for exchange. However, I wish to underline that when we had all come out and we were ready to leave, Mr. Aleksovski said that our departure was being delayed indefinitely because, in his words, the army had not done its share of the deal, apparently. Of course, we were all disappointed. We went back to the cells. Some 20 minutes later, orders came that we should go into the corridor again. Mr. Aleksovski then told us that Mr. Dario Kordic had intervened and ordered that we should be sent for exchange. That was how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you, in fact, that very day exchanged, or were you taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately we were boarded into this van and taken back to Vitez and put up in the cinema hall. And if I may continue, two hours later, two HVO soldiers appeared. They called out one young man called Suad Salkic, he said that they were his neighbours and not to be afraid, they had just come to see him. However, when that young man went out, we could hear them fighting, and then two other guards, policemen, HVO policemen, appeared who were at the door to the cinema hall, at the main entrance. Then these two men had a half a metre long pole and they were beating Suad Salkic with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that yourself, Mr. Surkovic, personally?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that, as did the other members of the group of 13 of us that were there. Suad Salkic was bleeding because one of the men had hit him on the back of the head here, and there was a cut, and it was bleeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO military police who came to heed the call assist Mr. Salkic?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they assisted, but I saw that he had been hit with this pole, and I saw the pole. I thought it could have serious consequences, so I asked the policemen to take him to the medical centre, which was 200 metres away from the cinema hall. I saw that these young men were terrified. They just shrugged their shoulders and didn't dare do anything, so that Salkic was left there in the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Mario Cerkez appeared in the cinema hall following this event?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Ms. Somers, could we know, could we learn from the witness whether he knew or whether he heard why Suad Salkic was beaten? What were the reasons for the treatment he was given?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was going to come following the next question. It's part of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've heard the question of His Honour. If you could explain about the appearance of Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: May I explain? Suad Salkic told us that those men were his neighbours. However, let me now explain this and the second part of the question. Some 40 minutes after that incident, Mr. Santic, Ivica, who was the mayor of Vitez, Mr. Mario Cerkez, Mr. Stipo Krizanac, and the late Boro Ilic, came to the cinema. They spoke to us -- that is, Mr. Ivica Santic insisted that the 13 of us should go back to our apartment. He told us if we agreed to go back, then within two hours he would have our apartments vacated, because some other people had already moved in. I asked, "How safe would we be if we stayed in Vitez?" The mayor told us that our security was equal to his and that nothing worse could happen to us than to him. I was angry about this whole thing. Then I showed Mr. Santic and Mr. Cerkez the wound on Mr. Salkic's head, which was bleeding, and my handkerchief was full of blood. Mr. Cerkez was very angry, and he said he would investigate. He went out, came back ten minutes later, and told us that those men were living close to Suad Salkic in the Sadovaca village, and that somebody had wounded with a firearm the mother of one of the guys who had beaten Mr. Salkic. I said, "But Mr. Salkic has nothing to do with that. He could have no influence over that." I'm not even sure that that was true, that the mother of one of the soldiers had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Cerkez indicate that he would take any measures to investigate and/or to punish the individuals who did this beating?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Cerkez said nothing further, and Mr. Ivica Santic was extremely embarrassed at that time. However, for us who were planned for exchange, this was a sign, and we insisted, in fact, we insisted that our families go with us and the families of a few other people who had still not left Vitez. And I say thank God that we left, because those who believed that they would be safe, many of them are under the ground. I know five or six such families who believed, but later were killed, a month or two later, and all trace of those families is lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, then, although you and the other gentlemen with you saw the beating take place, and Mr. Cerkez and Mr. Santic were aware of this, did they ever ask you to give a statement or to provide any details about what happened, either Cerkez or Santic or Mr. Krizanac? Did anybody ask you to provide any details about what happened, for purposes of investigating?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't make any record of that. They no longer insisted that we go back to our own apartments, because they, themselves, had seen the condition of Mr. Salkic, and they saw that we were determined to leave Vitez. Therefore my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did you ever learn of any investigation or punishment at any time subsequent being undertaken?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard of any investigation, but as a person, I hadn't expected that, because there were many far worse cases, many deaths. Compared to what happened later, in May, June, and July, this was a minor episode, a negligible one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, one question I neglected to ask you: Does the name "Milivoj Petkovic" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of that name for the first time in Busovaca. When we were about to be exchanged, we had to sign a document, on an A4 document. I think he was one of the HVO commanders, because it said in that document, "By order of Mr. Milivoj Petkovic" the 13 of us had to go for exchange. That was the first time I came across the name of Mr. Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask the usher please to present Exhibit Z2713.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, can you please explain what this document is and what authority it provided?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fuad Kaknjo was the president of the executive board, and the head was Ivan Santic. Mr. Kaknjo Fuad issued this document ordering me and Dzidic to accept refugees coming from Vitez, and as far as possible to facilitate their accommodation in the village in schools and camps and so on, and to assist them as far as we could with food, clothing, and so on. That was one of our tasks. This is a rather poor copy, but I think the original document is much clearer, and one can easily see the stamp and signature. That was my task for a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also engage in documenting the atrocities that took place in Vitez municipality from 1993 on, or perhaps slightly earlier?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the very first day of the conflict between the army and the HVO -- that is, the 20th of October, 1992, onwards, and even a little earlier on -- I kept a diary in which I took note of everything of importance. This is the duty I performed, to take care of refugees. Through those activities I learned a great deal about what had happened in Vitez, about the disappearance of entire families. From family members I collected invaluable information and data which made it possible for me to write a book about the conflict in Vitez, or rather Vitez from 1990 until 1995. In this book I covered some tragic situations, both among Croats and Muslims, but there is a great deal of evidence there, and this document made it possible for me to obtain some invaluable information, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your appointment to the commission, that you just indicated is evidenced on the document in front of you, did that appointment also facilitate your ability to collect this information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He just said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me; I read it wrong. I'd like to ask the usher to present Exhibit Z2715, and then the translation thereof, which would be Z2715A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, if I can ask you briefly to explain the items that are in this document and explain, again briefly, how they were collected and what use they have been put to?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: On the first page, document 681792, under point 5, the names are given of the camps where certain Muslim families were held. These figures on the number of incarcerated people, people under arrest, are approximations. They were obtained from people who were in the camps who were in the Brotherhood and Unity elementary school. And if you add up these figures, in these six collection points, there were roughly 1.200 to 1.500 people who were in captivity in Vitez. I must also point out that at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Just a moment. I think that the question put to you was not regarding the contents of the document itself that we have, but rather to tell us what this document is, where it comes from and what its purpose is. The question had to do with the form of the document rather than the contents. The contents we have before us, and we're going to read them.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: These are lists of names of people killed in that period in Vitez, in the local community, the date and place of birth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Wait a minute, please, Mr. Surkovic. What is this document? Can you define it for us? It was produced by you in front of a commission to be used for a certain purpose. Could you introduce the document? Not the contents of the document; the document as such.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a list of people who were killed in Vitez. The purpose was for people who had fled from Foca, Visegrad, so their families should know, to be able to trace them, whether they were killed or not. This list of names was also given to Mr. Mustafa Ahmic, who was a person in charge of the records. It is an authentic and trustworthy one. It is quite accurate regarding the list of dead people from Vitez and the refugees who were in the territory of Vitez on that date, in that period. I should also like to underline that regarding the Kolonija in Vitez, there are certain minor omissions, but these can and will be corrected. In my book, everything is accurate. This applies in particular to the Mujicic family, Kasim Mujicic and his children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they listed specifically in this document, Mr. Surkovic, the Mujicic family?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: This list mentions them here in one place. Kasim Mujicic, his granddaughter, and so on. But more precise data are missing, date of birth and the place where they were buried, because at the time I didn't have those data. But he was a man who was town mayor of Vitez for twelve years. Anyway, one is duty-bound to give exact data to families whose members were killed in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Mujicic family, on the page the last four numbers of which are 1800, which also lists the family Tuco and Kargic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The Mujicic family, it says here. Kasim, Nedim; Nedim was a pupil of mine. He is probably Mr. Dario Kordic's generation. He was killed sometime in July, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we can ask the usher to present exhibits 2714 and 2714A, and then 2714,1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are these documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: They are summaries that were made by the witness in the course of his serving on the commission that document the types of -- the nature of the death, the location, the villages. There are photographs, as well, of the places which were destroyed in the course of the conflicts that took place in Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking quickly, Mr. Surkovic, at the document labelled 2714,1, if you could just quickly explain to the Court what these photographs represent -- again, generically, what types of incidents were covered -- and then we'll move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: This is evidence of the crimes committed in Vitez in 1993. You see here an UNPROFOR soldier burying -- carrying bodies of killed people. You see the mosque; you see the pictures of people who were killed. All this is contained in my book. You see here children and women and the elderly; they were all killed in that tragic, unfortunate year in Vitez municipality. I wish to immemorialise those people. I want their children to know what happened, not to take revenge, but just so that they should know what war is. There were people of Croatian ethnicity who were killed too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, I going to interrupt you for a moment. Mr. Stein, have you seen these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The short answer is, the majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm just looking at 2714, and I see it begins with a list of people killed in Ahmici. There is then a hand-written text.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Surkovic. Well, we'll take the adjournment now. I hope it's going to be possible to complete this witness's evidence today. There's nothing in the summary about these documents. We'll take them out and consider them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. After attempting to get these in, Your Honour, that will be the end of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So I make sure we've got it right, we've got 2714, beginning with the list of people killed in Ahmici; we've got 2714,1, which are the photographs which have been attached; we've got 2715, the document which has already been referred to. Is that right? Is that what we should have?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and there will also be a request to have 2283A, which has already been admitted as the template for the translation of death certificates, which has been admitted in the testimony of other witnesses, so I don't think it is necessary to resubmit it, just to bring the Court's attention to it. Then Z1583 is the groups of death certificates specifically from Ahmici, which are essentially referenced and incorporated into the report, and the translations thereof. Much of this was attached to the statements which were turned over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The reason I was quizzical, Judge, is the photographs that we have look like this (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The quality is very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I can't tell you whether I've seen any of these before or not, because all I've seen was -- there's more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for a quarter of an hour now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Somers, we've looked at this. I think that this is the first such list that we've had in this case, is that right, of the people killed in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point we want to get home to the Prosecution is we do not want repetition of evidence. Now, do you want to rely on this as your evidence about the people who were killed in Ahmici or have you got other evidence which you want to call on the subject?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This particular list may be virtually identical to the list that was presented through another witness in a sister case. I would ask that it be accepted so that if any names may have inadvertently been left off of another list that is before the Court, it will give the Court a complete picture, based on the documentation that was gathered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is there any relationship between 2714, the list, and the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There should be names of some of the individuals. Now, this appears to be -- excuse me one second. 2714 is the actual Ahmici killing. Some of the photographs -- the Kargic family was not killed, as I understand it, at Ahmici. Some of the photographs that were turned in are more expansive or cover Vitez municipality beyond Ahmici, and I think the relevance for other deaths in the municipality is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Then there is, in the middle, a hand-written text. At page 5 of the document, there's a hand-written text. What is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document was, in the course of collecting documentation, was given to Mr. Surkovic by the mother of the infant whose death is described in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So these documents are being put in as documents collected by this witness in the course of his duties when he was collating evidence about these events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That is correct, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the basis upon which they are put in. I see. The pictures, similarly, are those he collected. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The last exhibit which I had indicated prior to the recess is the group of death certificates from Ahmici, or as many of them as this institution has been able to collect, that the witness has confirmed match his documentation. He had an opportunity to look through them. I would ask that we submit the exhibit as a composite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this the document which has already been exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The one that was exhibited was the top of it, the 2283A, which is a standard template translation into English for death certificates. The names on 1583 should correspond to 2714A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, we object to this kind of gathering of evidence. The witness did not state that it was his duty in accordance with the authorisation signed by Fuad Kakjno. He just used that opportunity to do these tasks privately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's an expression. I said it was part of his duty. No doubt you could ask him how he came to do it when you cross-examine. These are documents which he's collected, and it's on that basis which they are being submitted. Now, are you objecting to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, because they are part of a private investigation and not part of an official duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What difference does that make?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) We didn't hear about the sources, where these documents come from, the lists. I haven't heard that, at least. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You'll have the chance, Mr. Naumovski, to ask about where they came from. We shall admit them, the witness having collected them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I just, so there is no confusion, the last -- (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mrs. Somers, all that is stated here, has all of it been translated, including the hand-written document, because it is important. It is important that all the text, apart from photographs, be translated. Together with Mr. Stein, I must agree that some of the photographs are not quite visible, but he may come to that in the cross-examination. But in any event, have all the texts here been translated? That is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My understanding is there is a complete packet of translation in Exhibit 2714A, so it should be with the Court. If I could make it clear just for the Court that the last exhibit, 1583, are official documents that were shown to the witness to confirm that they match the information which he produced in his own work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. It was wisely pointed out that I have not submitted them to the Court. I've mentioned them, but I would ask the usher to please take the death certificates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mrs. Somers, perhaps you could tell us, at least, whether these death certificates are of those people who were killed, according to the list that was given to us, people who were apparently killed in Vitez. What are these death certificates that you're giving us, because just by giving us those death certificates, in themselves, they don't mean much. What are they related to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, these certificates relate to the deaths which occurred in Ahmici, and in the course of reading the other documents which are before you, you will see that there are other matters related to Donja Veceriska and Gacice and other villages. But these particular certificates relate to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How many, please, are there, just so we have that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to do a quick count, unless we have a summary figure. Judge, I did not itemise them. Shall I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to count them during the cross-examination, you can tell us how many there are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
