utterances.text: Thank you. Based on the information that I have had at my disposal, this is the end of my examination. I wanted to let the Court know that during the recess, the translation section presented a draft examination of the document which was discussed earlier at the beginning of the session, and we have presented it to counsel of both accused, and we have been told by the translation section -- and this is the first time we have seen it as well -- that tomorrow they expect to have the revised, proper translation for submission. Since I have not had the benefit of it either, I cannot proceed on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just to let the Court know, the translation reflects the glitch that occurred. The name of the witness is Surkovic, and it was written on the document as "Surkrovic" and did not come up in any prior searches. Therefore, we all suffered and paid the price, because it never surfaced. When we got it, we turned it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the statement to which Mr. Stein was referring?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, I would like to take you back to the beginning of your testimony, when you went to the basement along with, you said, Croats and Muslims, having heard the HVO approaching. There was a knock on the door. You started to go to the door to open the door, but the wife of Franjo Franjic said to you, "Don't go," and she went and opened the door. I wanted to find out, the wife of Franjo Franjic, to what ethnic group did she belong?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: She was a Croat, so a person of Croat nationality. She was in the neighbourhood. We were friends. We got on very well, and she was probably afraid that something may happen to me. She said it was the war and it was chaos, so she felt it was better for her to open the door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's why you allowed her to go, because she was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I thought that it would be wiser to let her open the door, because I knew that this was an HVO attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, we would like to switch the order of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic: Good day, Mr. Surkovic. My name is Goran Mikulicic, and I am representing Mario Cerkez. I would like to ask you several questions, so I would please ask you to respond according to your best recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, could you please tell us what your citizenship was in 1992 before the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared, and what was your nationality after the declaration of independence?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if you can tell the difference between Muslims with a capital "M" or with a small "m." If you notice the difference, then it will be clear to you. And you probably also know --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Surkovic. Would you please answer my question?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I was a Muslim with a capital "M." It may not be quite clear to you, but if you allow me to explain --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, would you please allow me to ask you this question again? Perhaps you didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I did understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will repeat the question: Up until April 1992, what was your citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: From April 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Until April 1992, I was a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that date?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I continued to be a citizen of that State.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was all that I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Mikulicic, I should like to remind you, for the benefit of the organisation of the discussion during the hearing, that we have already asked you why you keep asking the question of citizenship, and you told us. Perhaps we could gain time if we knew why you are asking it, because then you wouldn't have to ask the same question each time. You told us, regarding the nature of the conflict, we took note of that, and I think that in future, we could economise with that type of question and save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour for the suggestion. The Defence is aware of the fact that repeating a question does not lead to faster proceedings. Regarding this fact, Defence has requested from the Prosecution to admit this, not to dispute this. But until the Prosecution does not contest this, that this is a matter of the same citizens in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Defence would like to have the right to question that in each particular case. Because according to the Defence, this is a very important circumstance which establishes the basis for the application of the law. If Your Honours consider that at the time of the conflict that we are discussing now, all persons on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina were citizens of the same State, then there is no need for the Defence to keep on asking the same question. As far as the Defence understands, the Prosecution did not wish to stipulate this as a contested fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, in response to the Prosecutor's question, you stated that you were a Bosniak of Islamic faith by nationality; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you are a practising Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Surkovic -- and I think you said that yourself, that before the outbreak of the conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and before the multi-party elections, you were a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. In that political party, were you able to articulate your religious position?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: In the League of Communists, the League of Communists accepted people who did not visit religious objects, facilities, according to the concept of Tito's Yugoslavia. But you know very well that the party allows for -- the SDP party allows for religious freedom. I am a member of the SDP party, and that party allows me to have religious freedom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were a member of the League of Communists, did you also visit religious facilities?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not, but my father always went, and I always would greet my father in the Muslim manner out of respect for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Surkovic. Would you please tell us in what part of Vitez was your house, the house that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how familiar you are with Vitez. That is Street Partizanska Number 2, and it's the second house close to the hotel. It's Partizanska Street, two houses away from the petrol station. That's the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the name of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, we heard information about your job, and we can conclude from that that you spent a lot of time working as a professor in Vitez. How long, in fact, did you live in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: About 20 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be said that during your stay in Vitez, through your duties as professor, you practically met all the young men who attended high school?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not all of them. I didn't teach all of them. The high-school centre is large, and it would number from 900 and more students, so I didn't teach everybody. I didn't teach chemistry. But I did teach a large number of the young men who attended the high schools, and also all the vocational courses that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, you said that you also taught Mr. Kordic. Did you also teach Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did teach Mr. Kordic, but I don't remember Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Cerkez from any other context before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Personally, I know Mr. Tugomir Cerkez; that's Mario's father. I know his mother. But I know that Mr. Cerkez worked in the security service of the Unis factory, where I worked for a while. He worked with Mr. Sefkija Dzidic. I think that Mr. Cerkez has attended the reserve officers' school, and I think that his ability to work in the security service comes from that education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you said, Mr. Surkovic, that you knew Mr. Cerkez's parents very well. In socialising with those people, did you notice that they had any kind of religious or nationalistic leanings?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never noticed that they were chauvinistic in any way, or that they did not like any kind of national group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, you described the events on the morning of the 16th of April, 1994, and then you mentioned that together with your family, you went to the basement of the building. The basement was your shelter. Could you please tell us if you went down to the shelter before that day?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it happened once before, when a group of two or three aeroplanes of the former Yugoslav army was flying over Vitez. They bombed. They did not hit too many targets, but that was when we went to the shelter. All of the residents in the building went to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you correct me if I'm wrong, but the basement was suitable for use as a shelter from before, so in view of the fact that you used it before, you went downstairs to the basement again to seek refuge; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, after that, you told us about your encounter with the soldier in your apartment. You said that he was masked?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you noticed any kind of military insignia on the uniform of that young man?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: That young man, I said a moment ago, he had a stocking over his head. As for insignia, he just had the chequerboard flag and the HVO. I saw nothing more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice, on any other soldiers that you came across in your building on that day, the military insignia in addition to the fact that they carried the insignia of the HVO as an armed organisation?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, after that, you told us that you were taken to the Workers' University and put up in the basement there. You also told us that that building was secured by members of the HVO police. My question is, are you thinking of the military police or the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Surkovic, those soldiers, members of the military police, were they wearing any insignia by which you could tell that they were members of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms. The civilian police have their regular uniforms, and I knew a great many of them personally, so that I'm quite sure that this was the military police. That was their job. On the uniform, it said "Police," for the regular police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. We know of what happened with you later, when you were transferred to the chess club, to Kaonik, and back again. Let me ask you the following: Who was responsible for your transfer from the basement of the Workers' University to the chess club, then from the chess club to Kaonik? Who were those people who took care of you and who guarded you?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to underline that Mr. Zdravko Jurcevic was one of the persons in charge of security in Automobil, and he transferred a group of us from the Workers' University to the chess club, some 600 metres, by orders of Mr. Zlatko Nakic. And Mr. Jurcevic did so, unwillingly. In my presence, they quarrelled, but he followed orders nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. When you were in Kaonik, were there any guards there?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were the security guards. What is more, a young man who used to be my pupil was there who behaved very correctly. I do not wish to mention his name. I asked that young man to pretend not to know me, but I also asked him, if he could, to prevent the entry of military persons into the cell. In that way he would be assisting me most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this young man you are referring to, was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but my former student, and he found it very hard to accept what was happening in Vitez and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the military police? Could you tell us that? Or was he a member of another unit? Or perhaps you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wore a uniform. He was dressed in an HVO uniform. He did his job, but I didn't see the word "Police" written on his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Surkovic, if I understood you correctly, you stayed in the basement of the Workers' University for how many days?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there for three or four days, and then I was transferred to the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there, did anyone come to visit you? I'm referring to doctors or representatives of the international community: the Red Cross, the European monitors, or the like.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: We prisoners were entitled to be examined by a doctor, Dr. Franjo Tibold. And Dr. Rada Savanovic, a lady doctor, and another lady doctor, came one day to examine prisoners who needed treatment. As for the International Red Cross, I know that those people came to Busovaca and that I was registered by the International Red Cross; that is, I, together with the other 13 who were transferred there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, were you personally examined by Dr. Franjo Tibold?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask for any medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say you didn't ask for any medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, some other people needed the assistance of the doctor -- people who were suffering, who were old, who were weak -- and they needed assistance much more than I did. I personally didn't need any assistance. But I did need it in Busovaca, and I was given it in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I should like to ask the usher to help me to distribute some documents which the Defence would like to show to the witness and tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, I'm going to show you a list, and I am going to ask you to comment on that list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D29/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, will you please look at the back side of the yellow document and tell me whether you see Dr. Franjo Tibolt's name and his signature? Is he the person that you said came to examine people at the time you were in the basement of the Workers' University?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Franjo Tibolt excellently, and this is a list of people who were spared labour. But I wish to underline that I never asked to be relieved of labour. I asked representatives of the international organisation to protect us from the digging of trenches, because I had experience from Vitez that some people who were taken from the basement to dig trenches were killed there, and I was afraid of killings. As for labour, my name is on this list, but I wish to say that Mr. Tibolt did not examine me, nor did I ask him to examine me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Surkovic, during your stay as an internee, were you ever forced to do any compulsory labour?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Not once was I forced to dig trenches or dugouts, but I do know people who were, and I know people who were killed digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, while you were in the Workers' University, did a representative of the ECMM, people in white, come?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but I didn't talk to them. I was in the basement at the time. The people toured the cinema hall. But Mr. Bahtija Sivro told me that they had come, but I didn't talk to them. But I did talk to them in Busovaca on behalf of my group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people that we're talking about, the European Monitors, did they visit only the cinema hall or did they go downstairs to the basement?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the basement. They visited the cinema hall. However, I didn't speak to them because I spent the first three or four days in the basement. There were some prisoners on the upper floor in three rooms of the Workers' University as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You told us, Mr. Surkovic, that while you were in Kaonik, you requested to be examined by a doctor, and that you were taken to the health centre in Busovaca, where you were treated by a doctor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the circumstances under which you were taken to Busovaca? Were you transported in a closed vehicle, was it a truck, was it a private car; how did you travel from Kaonik to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a private car, a passenger car. There was a driver and one armed man next to me from the HVO police. If you need any further details, I can provide them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm interested in I will ask you. Were you alone in that car or was anyone else with you?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was alone on that occasion. In front was the driver, and next to me was an armed security guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of medical treatment was given to you in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I had some problems with my spine. I came across Dr. Josipovic and a nurse whose name I cannot recollect, but I know that the doctor was upset by what was happening. He prescribed all the necessary medicine. He was very polite in dealing with me. I asked him to somehow spare me from the digging of trenches, and I think that his findings were respected, though I wish to underline that from my cell or from the other two cells, no one was taken to dig trenches among us 13. None of us 13 were taken there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Surkovic. In connection with your injury, was this a previous injury or an injury you sustained while staying in Kaonik or in the Workers' University?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it is an earlier injury. I have problems with my back occasionally, but I think the fact that I stayed in the basement contributed to those problems with my back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Surkovic, when you were about to be released, as you told us, following orders of Milivoj Petkovic, Ivica Santic and some other men came to see you, you said that Ivica Santic was the mayor of Vitez, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it true that he represented the civilian authorities in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you understood me well. Mr. Santic came to the cinema hall when we were transferred from Busovaca, if that is how you understood it. Mr. Santic should have represented the civilian authorities because he was the mayor of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Surkovic, that all those talks and discussions over the release were conducted with Mr. Santic, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as those discussions on the release of people, I can't say who participated in them because I wasn't present. I didn't inform myself after that who conducted the negotiations, but I personally think that it was the military structures that agreed on the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Surkovic, I apologise if I was not quite clear in my question. My question was under these circumstances in the cinema hall, was Mr. Santic the person with whom the modalities and conditions of your release were discussed? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the cinema hall there were no discussions as to the ways in which we would be released. All this had been agreed beforehand, before we were transferred. Actually, we shouldn't have gone to the cinema hall. We were told to go there to sign a paper there, but then they said some other things needed to be settled before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back for a moment, Mr. Surkovic, to the incident that you described when a Bosniak was beaten up in the premises. You told us that he himself said that he was being called by two of his neighbours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The man's name was Suad Salkic. He was with me in Busovaca. He is the 13th man. He has a master's degree in electrical engineering. He was born in the village of Podgorica. We were scared when we saw these men in uniform calling him and we feared the worst, but he said to us, "Don't worry. They are my neighbours. I'm going to talk to them. They probably have something to tell me." But to our utter surprise, we heard them fighting, we heard shuffling and cries, and we heard this going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Tell me, while you stayed in those premises, were there any other such incidents of soldiers beating any of the Bosniaks who were there?

utterances.speaker: ENES SURKOVIC
utterances.text: The rest of the time I spent there, no such thing happened. But I must underline that the cinema hall had walls, and I asked these people to intensify the security because I was afraid that somebody might throw in a hand grenade. I think that Mr. Santic and Mr. Cerkez took certain steps. We didn't sleep. We were afraid that somebody might throw in a hand grenade. We heard, on several occasions in front of the cinema hall, soldiers' boots, so people were probably marching there. They probably accepted our suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, in view of the time, I have a few more questions, a whole set of questions relating to the documents admitted today, of which he is the author. My suggestion would be, with your permission, that I continue with those questions tomorrow. As for this particular topic, I have finished my examination. Of course, if that suits Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you shorten your cross-examination tomorrow, if you have some time to prepare it, Mr. Mikulicic. Very well, we'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour had asked for a count of the documents, and my two colleagues on two counts have come up with 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Surkovic, I'm afraid your evidence hasn't finished today. Could you be back tomorrow, please, at the same time, half past 2.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, I'll be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you please remember this during the adjournment, not to speak to anybody about your evidence, and that does include members of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
